The Hundred · Mitts 0.3.17

The Hundred.
Cargo against Mitts, on 100 Rust projects.

One hundred open-source Rust projects, each built the way parallel branches and coding agents build: twelve worktrees of the same project at once. Plain cargo, cargo with sccache and Mitts, on three machines. Time, CPU, compiler runs and disk, measured, not estimated. No measured project is dropped from the totals (runs the harness flagged as noisy stay in, marked), and where Mitts is not faster, this page says so.

13 minwith Mitts to build 12 worktrees of each of 100 projects, 76 min with Cargo
3 hof processor time, what a laptop battery and a CI bill pay for, 20 h with Cargo
6,905compiler runs, 90,961 with Cargo: Mitts compiles a unit once and restores it everywhere else
111 GBwritten to disk, 641 GB with Cargo: restored files are linked or cloned, not rewritten

The big figures are the macOS machine, summed over its 100 projects. The other two machines are in the charts below, tool by tool.

The scoreboard

Totals over every measured project on each machine (100 on macOS and Linux aarch64 XFS, 90 on Linux x86_64 XFS), each project building 12 worktrees at once. The length of a bar is what it cost, on a plain linear scale. Red is Mitts. The big number on the right is how much Mitts saved against plain Cargo.

Time is wall-clock seconds of the 12-worktree build, summed over the measured projects. CPU is user plus system seconds of every process. Compiler runs counts rustc invocations. Disk written is what reached the block device. Disk in use is the peak size of all worktrees and the shared store, measured with du; du counts every copy-on-write clone as a separate file, so on XFS it drops far less than the bytes actually written (the Linux gain in disk in use is small because cloned files still count in full).

How long a project takes

Minutes and seconds, not ratios. Each project builds its tests in 12 worktrees at once. The top row is a typical project (the median of the machine’s projects, tool by tool); below it the slowest projects, where the difference is largest. Bars start at zero on a plain linear scale and the number is the measured time.

Every project, one row

Every measured project, slowest with Cargo first. Grey is plain Cargo, red is Mitts, both from zero on the same linear scale, and the measured value is written at the end of each row. Pick a machine and a measure. Short rows are projects that build in seconds; the numbers still tell them apart.

Cargo with a warm sccache cuts CPU but wall time only a little: sccache still starts a wrapper for every rustc call, does not cache linking, and Cargo still runs every build script. Both are in the scoreboard and the project tables.

What was tested, and how

The Hundred
100 open-source Rust projects from crates.io and GitHub, fixed in scripts/corpus_100.json. Measured projects per machine: 100 on macOS and Linux aarch64 XFS, 90 on Linux x86_64 XFS; every ratio is computed per machine over that machine’s own set. nushell is excluded. Projects Cargo itself cannot build are replaced so the corpus stays at 100.
The scenario
Twelve git worktrees of one project, on 4 different commits, all build the project’s tests at the same moment. That is what parallel branches, a review queue or a team of coding agents does. Test execution is the same for every tool and is not timed; the build uses test --no-run.
The tools
Plain Cargo, Cargo + sccache (sccache 0.17.0) and Mitts 0.3.17 (commit 045c5cd241c0, binary SHA-256 01408cb9aed29601fb20c7bfa2f1675c501dd6cbcf96defe4996eecb7eaed394). Same toolchain, same machine, Cargo arms run --offline. A shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR was also run as a demonstration and is left out of the charts: it either missed the injected failure or leaked it into clean worktrees, so it is unsound.
The five readings
Wall-clock time of the swarm; CPU time (user + system of all processes); compiler runs; bytes written to the device; peak disk in use. Each is the median of 3 repeats; quartiles are in the raw data.
Soundness
Worktree 12 gets one deliberately failing test. A tool counts only if all 12 worktrees compile with test --no-run and produce the same number of test binaries as plain Cargo. After the timed build, an untimed smoke run filtered to that test checks that worktree 12 fails on it and that a clean worktree runs its test binaries with no failure. A shared target directory fails this check.
A quiet machine
Before each run the machine must be idle: CPU busy fraction and load under a threshold and no foreign compiler process. File systems are synced before disk readings.
Totals and typical projects
The scoreboard sums each reading over the projects of one machine. The “typical project” rows are the median over the projects, tool by tool. Every measured project is in the scoreboard and in the medians. The harness flagged 7 project runs as noisy (the 3 repeats of a swarm differed by more than 15%); they are marked “wide spread” in the project table and kept. A scenario row can cover fewer projects than the swarm: the edit probe fails to compile on crates that deny missing docs, and a few projects fail check or clippy on lints already present upstream, under every tool. Each row lists its project count.
Provenance
Every result file records the binary hash, the hash of each script, the commit, the toolchain, the file systems and the load before each run. The reduced data, with absolute paths and device names removed, is in the repository: docs/data/benchmarks.json.

The other scenarios

The swarm is the case Mitts was built for. The same study also measured everyday builds. Each row is a typical project on the chosen machine (the median over the projects, tool by tool), in real time, from zero on a linear scale; every row has its own scale, so compare the three bars within a row, not rows with each other.

Where Mitts does not win

A single cold build of one checkout, with an empty store, has nothing to reuse and also pays to hash the inputs and fill the store for later builds. So the cold row above is the one where plain Cargo is as fast or a little faster: plain Cargo finished first on 66–77% of the projects, depending on the machine. Cargo + sccache starts cold with an empty cache too, and pays for its wrapper and cache writes, so Mitts is ahead of it there.

What these numbers do and do not say

  • One version. All three machines ran 0.3.17. Mitts has changed since; each series stands on its own and numbers from different versions are not compared.
  • Reuse is the point. The swarm and second-worktree scenarios measure what a shared store buys when the same code is built many times. They are not the cost of a single first build, which the cold-build rows show.
  • Totals favour big projects. A sum is dominated by the slowest projects. The per-project chart and the typical-project rows show the spread.
  • Three repeats. Medians of three runs are stable for these workloads but not a confidence interval. The quartiles are in the data.
  • Desktop noise. The Mac Studio carried resident agent sessions during its run. The idle check records and bounds this; it does not remove it.
  • No-op rebuild. “Build again, nothing changed” is Mitts with its fast lock on, as a plain mitts build runs it. The harness passes an explicit --cache-dir, which turns the fast lock off; with it off the same step is about four times faster than Cargo instead of ten to nineteen (the figure is in the raw data as noop_cache_dir_ms).
  • Memory. Memory is the peak resident size of the heaviest compiler or linker process in a worktree, and its sum over the 12 worktrees. A detached sccache server is outside the measured processes.
  • Disk figures. Device bytes written are whole-device counters and compare tools within one run, not across machines.
  • Not covered. Windows, cross-compilation and a remote or team cache are not supported yet and not measured.
